blocks.text: The same real world fact can end up looking like a dozen different values inside one dataset. A country column might contain USA, usa, U.S.A., United States, and us, all describing the exact same country, just typed differently by different people at different times. To a human reading the column, these are obviously the same thing. To pandas, and to any groupby, filter, or join built on top of that column, they are five completely unrelated strings.

This is what inconsistent data means, and it is one of the quieter kinds of dirty data because nothing looks broken at first glance. There are no NaN values to trip an isna() check, no duplicate rows for duplicated() to catch. The data is just fragmented across multiple spellings of the same underlying value, and every operation that depends on exact string matching, grouping customers by country, filtering for a specific category, joining two tables on a shared key, quietly produces the wrong answer without ever raising an error.
1. What Inconsistent Data Actually Means
Inconsistent data is the same underlying value represented in more than one way across rows in a column. It shows up in a few very common shapes.

items: Categorical spelling and casing variants, like 'USA', 'U.S.A.', 'United States', and 'us' all meaning the same country.
Categorical abbreviation variants, like 'M', 'Male', 'male', and 'm' all meaning the same gender category.
Format variants within the same column, like a date column that mixes '01/02/2023' and '2023-02-01' for two different rows.

blocks.text: 2. Why Inconsistent Data Creeps In
Inconsistency rarely comes from one bad decision, it usually comes from several reasonable decisions made in different places at different times.

items: Data merged from multiple sources. A CRM export might use 'United States' while a payments provider's export uses the ISO code 'US', and once the two tables are combined into one column, both spellings exist side by side.

Free text entry with no dropdown or validation. A signup form with a plain text country field will collect as many spellings as it has users, because there was never anything stopping someone from typing 'us' in lowercase.

Changes in data entry standards over time. A system that used to store 'M' and 'F' for gender might later switch to storing 'Male' and 'Female', and years of historical rows never get retroactively updated to match.

blocks.text: 3. Detecting Inconsistency with value_counts()

value_counts() on a categorical column is the single most useful first move for spotting inconsistency. It returns every distinct value in the column along with how many times each one appears, sorted from most common to least common, which means every spelling and casing variant surfaces in one glance instead of staying hidden inside a column that looks fine on the surface.

A healthy categorical column shows a short list of counts that add up sensibly. An inconsistent one shows the same real value split across several rows in the output, each with a suspiciously small count, which is exactly the signal to look for.

blocks.title: Read the whole output, not just the top rows
blocks.content: It is tempting to glance at the first few lines of value_counts() and move on, but the rare variant that only appears once or twice is usually sitting near the bottom of that output, not the top. Scrolling through the full list is what catches the version of a country name that showed up on exactly one row.

blocks.text: 4. Fixing Casing and Whitespace

Two of the most common sources of inconsistency have nothing to do with the actual word being used, they come from casing and stray whitespace that a human eye barely notices but a computer treats as a completely different string.
4.1 Case Normalization
str.lower() (or str.upper()) collapses every casing variant of a value down to one consistent form. 'USA', 'usa', and 'Usa' all become the same string once every character is lowercased.
4.2 Whitespace Stripping

str.strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace. 'USA' and 'USA ' look identical to a human reading a spreadsheet, but they are two different strings to a computer, and that trailing space is enough to make value_counts() and groupby() treat them as separate categories.
In practice these two fixes are almost always applied together, chained in a single line, since a column rarely has only one of these two problems and not the other.

blocks.title: Fixing only one of the two is a common trap
blocks.content: It is easy to run str.lower() on a column, see the value_counts() output look mostly clean, and stop there. But a value with trailing whitespace still shows up as a separate row after casing is fixed, since lowercasing does nothing to a space character. Always strip and normalize casing together, not one and not the other.

blocks.text: 5. Fixing with Mapping Dictionaries

Casing and whitespace fixes only collapse variants that differ purely in formatting. They do nothing for a column where 'us', 'usa', and 'united states' are genuinely different words that happen to mean the same thing. For that, the most reliable technique is an explicit mapping dictionary built by hand from what value_counts() showed you.

code.content:
country_map = {
    "us": "United States",
    "usa": "United States",
    "u.s.a.": "United States",
    "united states": "United States",
    "america": "United States",
}
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.lower().map(country_map)

blocks.text: .map() looks up every value in the dictionary and replaces it with the matching value, but anything not present as a key in the dictionary becomes NaN, which is worth knowing before running it on a column you have not fully reviewed. .replace() behaves more gently, since any value not found in the dictionary is simply left unchanged instead of being wiped out.

blocks.title: A mapping dictionary is only as good as the value_counts() review behind it
blocks.content: This technique is the most reliable one available because it is completely explicit, every input variant and its correct output are written down by hand. The tradeoff is that it only works for variants you actually noticed and included as keys. Anything missed silently falls through, either as NaN with map() or as an unchanged value with replace().

blocks.text: 5.1 Fuzzy Matching for Variants You Cannot List by Hand

A mapping dictionary works well when you can look at value_counts() and enumerate every variant yourself. For a column with dozens or hundreds of near duplicate spellings, typos included, writing out every key by hand stops being practical. This is where fuzzy matching comes in, grouping strings by how similar they are to each other using a similarity threshold, instead of requiring an exact key. Libraries like fuzzywuzzy and its faster successor rapidfuzz are the standard tools for this in Python.

code.content:
from rapidfuzz import process

choices = ["United States", "Canada", "United Kingdom"]
best_match, score, _ = process.extractOne("Untied States", choices)
# best_match is "United States", score reflects how close the match was

blocks.text: Fuzzy matching is genuinely useful, but it is also a more advanced technique that trades certainty for coverage, an aggressive similarity threshold can merge two values that were actually different. For most inconsistent columns in this course, an explicit mapping dictionary built from a full value_counts() review is the technique to reach for first.
6. Worked Example: Cleaning a Country Column
Say you load a customer table and the country column looks fine until you actually check it.

code.content:
data = {
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7],
    "country": ["USA", "usa", "U.S.A.", "United States", "us", "  USA", "Usa "],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df["country"].value_counts())
# USA               1
# usa               1
# U.S.A.            1
# United States     1
# us                1
#   USA             1
# Usa               1

blocks.text: Seven rows, seven distinct values, and every single one of them means the United States. value_counts() makes that immediately obvious, since a real dataset with seven genuinely different countries would never split its counts this evenly across near identical spellings.
Strip and lowercase first, then apply a mapping dictionary built from exactly the variants that showed up.

code.content:
country_map = {
    "usa": "United States",
    "u.s.a.": "United States",
    "united states": "United States",
    "us": "United States",
}
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.lower().map(country_map)
print(df["country"].value_counts())
# United States    7

blocks.text: Seven distinct strings collapsed into one, and every downstream operation, a groupby("country"), a filter for United States customers, a join against a country reference table, now behaves the way it was always supposed to.
7. Date Format Inconsistency

Dates deserve their own mention because the same column can silently mix multiple formats, and this particular kind of inconsistency is more dangerous than a misspelled country name, since a wrongly parsed date does not look wrong, it just looks like a different date.

01/02/2023 is genuinely ambiguous on its own. Under the US convention of month first, it means January 2nd. Under the day first convention used across most of Europe and much of the world, it means February 1st. Both readings are valid interpretations of the exact same string, and pandas has no way to know which one your data actually means unless you tell it.

blocks.title: Do not trust automatic date parsing blindly
blocks.content: Letting pd.to_datetime() guess a format on an ambiguous column can silently produce the wrong date for some rows and the right date for others, depending on which values happen to be unambiguous, like a day value above 12. The result looks perfectly valid, a real date with no error raised, which makes this a genuinely dangerous mistake to leave unchecked.

blocks.text: The fix is to be explicit. If you know the source of the dates, pass the exact format, or set dayfirst to match the convention that column was actually written in.

code.content:
pd.to_datetime("01/02/2023", format="%m/%d/%Y")   # January 2nd, month first convention
pd.to_datetime("01/02/2023", format="%d/%m/%Y")   # February 1st, day first convention

blocks.text: For a column that genuinely mixes multiple formats in different rows, pandas' format='mixed' option parses each value with whichever format fits it, while dayfirst still resolves the ambiguous cases consistently.
8. Common Mistakes

items: Fixing casing but forgetting whitespace, or the other way around. Both problems can exist in the same column at once, and fixing only one leaves the other quietly splitting your categories.
Skimming value_counts() instead of reading the full output, and missing a rare variant that only shows up on one or two rows as a result.
Building a mapping dictionary from memory instead of from what value_counts() actually returned, which is how a real variant sitting in the data ends up missing from the dictionary's keys.
Trusting pd.to_datetime() to guess a format on an ambiguous date column without checking whether the guess matches the convention the data was actually written in.

blocks.text: 9. Recap and Checklist

items: Run value_counts() on the column and read the entire output, not just the top rows.
Strip whitespace and normalize casing together with str.strip().str.lower().
Run value_counts() again to see what is left after formatting differences are removed.
Build an explicit mapping dictionary from the remaining distinct values and apply it with map() or replace().
For a column too large to map by hand, consider fuzzy matching with a tool like rapidfuzz, and review its output carefully.
For a date column, check whether more than one format is present, and parse it with an explicit format or dayfirst rather than trusting automatic parsing.
Run value_counts() one final time to confirm the column now holds exactly the distinct values it should.
